# Many dimensions on a flat screen

Data have many dimensions: the three of space, time, and each measured property (a count, a price, a temperature). A screen has two. The work is to choose which dimensions get the two axes, which get a different means, and which are dropped. This file is about that choice, in a chart and in a plan of a place.

## The eye completes a flat picture, in its own way

A flat picture has no depth. The eye adds depth from habit, and then holds on to what it added: a flat shape painted as a window is seen as a window that swings, also by a person who knows the trick.

- **Use this**: a view that the person knows from life is read with no explanation.
- **Do not work against it**: if a picture looks like a scene, it is read as a scene, and the person must then fight that reading to find the data.

## Give each dimension its own means

| The dimension | Means that carry it |
|---|---|
| a position or a distance | an axis; the place on a map |
| the time | an axis; the sequence along a path; rings from a center |
| an amount | the width of a band; the length of a bar; the count of equal marks, each for a fixed number |
| a group or a direction | a color |
| a second measured property | a second chart on the same axis, below the first |

- **One axis can carry two dimensions when they run together.** A flight drawn with the time along the bottom: the same axis is the distance flown, because the plane moves on. A thing that has a size in space (a cloud) can stand in that picture; the person does not take its width for a span of time.
- **The path of a march on a map**, the size of the army as the width of the band, the way there and the way back as two colors, and the temperature as a chart below on the same axis: four kinds of data in one picture, and the losses at each river are seen. This is the model to aim at when the data have a story.
- **Say which means carries which dimension**, at the picture, in words.
- **A count as a number of equal marks** (one stroke for 100 people) keeps the amount honest, where an area or an angle does not.

## Do not dress data as a scene

A chart of 100-meter records drawn as a running track, with a runner on it, reads as a race: one runner chases the other, and the dots look like people who did not finish. In fact the length of the "track" is the time and each lane is a decade. The person first believes the scene and then has to take it apart.

- **A chart that imitates the thing it is about is a warning sign.** The form of the data (axes, marks) and the look of the subject are two things; do not mix them.
- **A figure drawn to say which color is which** must not stand in a place where its position looks like a value.

## Drop a dimension

Which dimension does the person not need for this task? Drop it, and the picture gets simpler and has room for other things.

- **Three to two: a view from the side.** A plan from above is the usual form and not a natural one: people do not look at buildings from above, and the way between floors is hard to see on separate plans. A building that is one long hall, with nothing that changes in its depth, can be drawn from the front: all floors in one picture, with each escalator and where it leads.
- **A slanted pile of floor plans** shows less well which stair meets which. If the links between the floors matter, show them in a side view, and give the flat plan of each floor next to it for the way on the floor.
- **A side view of lifts and levels** is enough for step-free access in a station: which lift goes from which level to which. How each level looks is not needed; the signs on the level do that.
- **Two to one: a line.** For a route that nobody can leave (the stops of one line, the way through an airport from the door to the gate), only the sequence matters. Draw one straight line with the stops on it. The free dimension takes the changes to other lines, the times, or the load of each part.
- **A simple picture can work as two views at once**: a village on a hill, drawn so that it reads as a map and as the view from the boat.
- **A known thing keeps its known view**, also when the picture has a different one: a tower on a map from above is drawn from the side, because that is how people know it. The same holds for an icon: draw the part that tells what the thing is in the view where it is recognised.
- **A thing that is not where the picture puts it** (a train that leaves at a right angle to the hall) can stay simplified, if the person still goes to the correct part of the building.

## People learn the rules of a picture

People accept the rules of a flat world quickly, as in a game that is seen from the side. If a picture has an unusual rule, teach it by a first case that is so plain that it cannot be read wrongly, and then go to the harder ones.

## What to draw

- Axes for the two dimensions that the question is about, and a different means for each other one, named at the picture.
- A second chart on the same axis for a second property.
- A side view where the links between levels matter.
- A straight line for a route with no choice.
- No chart in the shape of its subject.
